views.name: trees_income_raw_join
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  t.tree_id AS tree_id,
  COALESCE(t.zipcode, it.zipcode) AS zip,
  t.boroname AS borough,
  it.Estimate_Median_income AS median_income,
  it.Estimate_Mean_income AS mean_income,
  -- pack all other tree fields as a JSON object to keep one column for remaining fields
  json_object(
    'idx', t.idx,
    'tree_dbh', t.tree_dbh,
    'stump_diam', t.stump_diam,
    'status', t.status,
    'health', t.health,
    'spc_latin', t.spc_latin,
    'spc_common', t.spc_common,
    'address', t.address,
    'borocode', t.borocode,
    'nta_name', t.nta_name,
    'state', t.state,
    'latitude', t.latitude,
    'longitude', t.longitude
  ) AS other_tree_fields
FROM trees t
LEFT JOIN income_trees it
  ON COALESCE(t.zipcode, it.zipcode) = it.zipcode
views.description: Combine the trees dataset with the income dataset by ZIP code to produce one unified row per tree record that includes income fields (median and mean) and borough, ensuring missing ZIP values are filled from the available source before/at join time if necessary.

views.name: clean_and_normalize_fields
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  tree_id,
  zip,
  CASE
    WHEN trim(lower(borough)) IN ('manhattan','new york','new york county','mn') THEN 'Manhattan'
    WHEN trim(lower(borough)) IN ('bronx','bronx borough','bx') THEN 'Bronx'
    WHEN trim(lower(borough)) IN ('brooklyn','kings','kings county','bk') THEN 'Brooklyn'
    WHEN trim(lower(borough)) IN ('queens','qn','queens borough') THEN 'Queens'
    WHEN trim(lower(borough)) IN ('staten island','richmond','staten island borough','si') THEN 'Staten Island'
    WHEN borough IS NULL OR trim(borough) = '' THEN NULL
    ELSE NULL
  END AS borough_canonical,
  CASE
    WHEN median_income IS NULL OR trim(median_income) = '' THEN NULL
    ELSE CAST(median_income AS NUMERIC)
  END AS median_income_num,
  CASE
    WHEN mean_income IS NULL OR trim(mean_income) = '' THEN NULL
    ELSE CAST(mean_income AS NUMERIC)
  END AS mean_income_num,
  other_tree_fields
FROM trees_income_raw_join
views.description: Clean and canonicalize the joined relation: normalize borough names (trim, null-empty canonicalization), coerce median_income and mean_income to numeric types, and mark or remove clearly invalid borough values. Do not apply the >0 filters here; only standardize and make fields query-ready.

views.name: trees_income_filtered
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  t.tree_id AS tree_id,
  t.zipcode AS zip,
  n.borough_canonical AS borough_canonical,
  n.median_income_num AS median_income_num,
  n.mean_income_num AS mean_income_num
FROM clean_and_normalize_fields n
JOIN trees t ON n.tree_id = t.tree_id
WHERE n.median_income_num > 0
  AND n.mean_income_num > 0
  AND n.borough_canonical IS NOT NULL
  AND trim(n.borough_canonical) <> ''
views.description: Filter the cleaned tree-income rows to only those with median_income_num > 0, mean_income_num > 0, and a non-null/non-empty/valid borough_canonical.

views.name: borough_tree_counts_and_mean_income
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  boroname AS borough_canonical,
  COUNT(*) AS tree_count,
  AVG(income_trees.Estimate_Mean_income) AS avg_mean_income,
  MIN(tree_id) AS any_tree_id
FROM
  trees
  LEFT JOIN income_trees ON trees.zipcode = income_trees.zipcode
GROUP BY
  boroname
views.description: For each borough (one row per borough), compute the count of tree records and the average of mean_income_num across the filtered tree-linked records. (Do not apply top-3 here; produce one row per borough.)

views.name: trees_raw_rows
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  tree_id,
  boroname AS borough,
  health
FROM trees
WHERE boroname IS NOT NULL
  AND TRIM(boroname) <> ''
  AND health IS NOT NULL
  AND TRIM(health) <> ''
views.description: Select the raw rows representing individual trees, keeping borough and health status as recorded. Exclude rows where borough or health status is NULL or missing so downstream counts are well-defined.

views.name: trees_in_bronx
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  tree_id,
  health
FROM
  trees
WHERE
  boroname = 'Bronx'
views.description: Filter the raw tree rows to only those located in the Bronx (borough equals Bronx). Keep each tree as one row with its health value for numerator/denominator calculations.

views.name: bronx_counts_by_health
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  health AS health,
  COUNT(*) AS count_by_health,
  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM trees WHERE boroname = 'Bronx') AS bronx_total_count
FROM trees
WHERE boroname = 'Bronx'
GROUP BY health
views.description: Aggregate the Bronx tree rows to produce counts per health status and the total count of trees in the Bronx. Do not collapse health when producing the per-health counts; also produce an overall total for the borough.

views.name: bronx_good_percentage
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  'Bronx' AS borough,
  CASE
    WHEN bronx_total_count = 0 THEN 0.0
    ELSE (CAST(SUM(CASE WHEN health = 'Good' THEN count_by_health ELSE 0 END) AS REAL) / bronx_total_count) * 100.0
  END AS percentage_good
FROM (
  SELECT health, count_by_health, bronx_total_count
  FROM bronx_counts_by_health
)
views.description: Combine the per-health counts and the borough total to compute the proportion/percentage of trees whose health status is 'Good'. This final step uses the counts computed earlier to calculate (count where health = Good) / (bronx_total_count) * 100.

views.name: year_filtered_records
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  ci.industry AS industry,
  cd.year_founded AS year,
  1 AS new_unicorn_count,
  cd.company_id AS row_id
FROM companies_dates cd
JOIN companies_industries ci
  ON cd.company_id = ci.company_id
WHERE cd.year_founded IN (2019, 2020, 2021)
views.description: Select rows restricted to the years 2019, 2020, and 2021. Keep the industry and the count of new unicorn companies (one row per original record).

views.name: industry_year_aggregation
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  ci.industry AS industry,
  cd.year_founded AS year,
  COUNT(DISTINCT cd.company_id) AS new_unicorns_in_year
FROM companies_industries ci
JOIN companies_dates cd USING (company_id)
GROUP BY ci.industry, cd.year_founded
views.description: Aggregate new unicorn company counts per industry per year (sum counts for same industry-year). Produces one row per industry-year with that year's total new unicorns for the industry.

views.name: industry_total_2019_2021
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  iya.industry AS industry,
  COALESCE(SUM(CASE WHEN iya.year IN (2019,2020,2021) THEN iya.new_unicorns_in_year END), 0) AS total_new_unicorns_2019_2021,
  json_group_array(json_object('year', iya.year, 'new_unicorns', iya.new_unicorns_in_year)) AS new_unicorns_by_year
FROM industry_year_aggregation AS iya
GROUP BY iya.industry
views.description: For each industry, sum the new unicorn counts across 2019, 2020, and 2021 to get the total new unicorns over the period. Produce one row per industry with the 3-year total and the per-year totals still available if needed.

views.name: top_industry_average
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  ci.industry AS industry,
  CAST(COALESCE(SUM(
    CASE
      WHEN substr(cd.date_joined,1,4) BETWEEN '2019' AND '2021' THEN 1
      ELSE 0
    END
  ),0) AS INTEGER) AS total_new_unicorns_2019_2021,
  -- average per year computed as total / 3; keep as numeric
  (CAST(COALESCE(SUM(
    CASE
      WHEN substr(cd.date_joined,1,4) BETWEEN '2019' AND '2021' THEN 1
      ELSE 0
    END
  ),0) AS REAL) / 3.0) AS average_new_unicorns_per_year,
  -- rank placeholder: compute rank over industries by total desc
  RANK() OVER (ORDER BY CAST(COALESCE(SUM(
    CASE
      WHEN substr(cd.date_joined,1,4) BETWEEN '2019' AND '2021' THEN 1
      ELSE 0
    END
  ),0) AS INTEGER) DESC) AS rank
FROM companies_industries ci
LEFT JOIN companies_dates cd
  ON ci.company_id = cd.company_id
GROUP BY ci.industry
views.description: Rank industries by their 2019-2021 total descending, select the top industry, and compute the average new unicorns per year for that top industry as (total_new_unicorns_2019_2021 / 3). Return the industry's name and the computed average.

views.name: pizza_recipe_toppings
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  pizza_recipes.pizza_id AS pizza_recipe_id,
  TRIM(topping_name) AS ingredient
FROM
  pizza_recipes,
  -- split toppings CSV into rows by leveraging recursive CTE pattern inline is not allowed here;
  -- instead use a join against pizza_toppings by matching ids present in the CSV list
  pizza_toppings
WHERE
  -- match topping_id against comma-separated list in pizza_recipes.toppings
  -- surround with commas to avoid partial matches (e.g., "1" matching "11")
  INSTR(',' || pizza_recipes.toppings || ',', ',' || CAST(pizza_toppings.topping_id AS TEXT) || ',') > 0
views.description: List the standard toppings (ingredients) for each pizza recipe (one row per pizza-topping association) so the recipe ingredients can be joined to order rows.

views.name: delivered_orders_or_pizzas
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  pco.order_id,
  pco.pizza_id,
  CASE
    WHEN pcr.cancellation IS NOT NULL AND TRIM(LOWER(pcr.cancellation)) <> '' THEN 'cancelled'
    WHEN pcr.cancellation IS NULL AND pcro.cancellation IS NOT NULL AND TRIM(LOWER(pcro.cancellation)) <> '' THEN 'cancelled'
    ELSE 'delivered'
  END AS delivery_status,
  -- prefer a pickup_time / order_time as delivery timestamp surrogate where available
  COALESCE(pcro.pickup_time, pcr.pickup_time, pco.order_time, pco.order_time) AS delivery_timestamp
FROM pizza_customer_orders pco
LEFT JOIN pizza_runner_orders pcr ON pco.order_id = pcr.order_id
LEFT JOIN pizza_clean_runner_orders pcro ON pco.order_id = pcro.order_id
WHERE
  -- Exclude rows that explicitly indicate cancellation or non-delivery status in any runner table text fields
  NOT (
    (pcr.cancellation IS NOT NULL AND TRIM(LOWER(pcr.cancellation)) <> '')
    OR (pcro.cancellation IS NOT NULL AND TRIM(LOWER(pcro.cancellation)) <> '')
  )
views.description: Select the set of pizza-order (or pizza-item) records that represent pizzas which were actually delivered to customers. This filters out orders/items that are cancelled, not delivered, in-progress, or otherwise not completed. Keep any identifiers needed to join to pizza composition/ingredient lines.

views.name: pizza_ingredient_lines
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  pr.pizza_id AS pizza_id,
  CAST(trim(tid) AS INTEGER) AS ingredient_id,
  pt.topping_name AS ingredient_name,
  NULL AS ingredient_quantity
FROM pizza_recipes pr,
     -- split the comma-separated toppings into rows by using recursive CTE-style CSV split emulation via instr/substr is not allowed here,
     -- instead use a simple approach: treat each topping token by replacing commas with a separator and iterating using sqlite's built-in functions is not available.
     -- To stay within a single SELECT and valid SQLite, we join against pizza_recipe_toppings view if present which exposes each ingredient token.
     pizza_recipe_toppings prt
JOIN (
  SELECT pizza_recipe_id, ingredient AS tid FROM pizza_recipe_toppings
) split ON split.pizza_recipe_id = pr.pizza_id
LEFT JOIN pizza_toppings pt ON CAST(trim(split.tid) AS INTEGER) = pt.topping_id
-- Use rows from pizza_recipe_toppings that correspond to this recipe's pizza_id
WHERE pr.pizza_id = split.pizza_recipe_id
views.description: All ingredient-on-pizza records (the composition lines) that record how much of each ingredient is used on a particular pizza, including the ingredient identifier, ingredient name (if present), and the per-pizza quantity field. Do not aggregate; one row per ingredient instance on a pizza.

views.name: delivered_pizza_ingredient_instances
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  d.order_id,
  d.pizza_id,
  p.ingredient_id,
  p.ingredient_name,
  p.ingredient_quantity
FROM delivered_orders_or_pizzas AS d
JOIN pizza_ingredient_lines AS p
  ON d.pizza_id = p.pizza_id
WHERE d.delivery_status = 'delivered'
views.description: Join delivered pizzas to their ingredient lines to produce only ingredient instances that belong to delivered pizzas. Preserve the per-pizza ingredient quantity for summation.

views.name: ingredient_totals
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  pi.ingredient_id AS ingredient_id,
  pi.ingredient_name AS ingredient_name,
  SUM(pi.ingredient_quantity) AS total_quantity
FROM pizza_ingredient_lines pi
GROUP BY
  pi.ingredient_id,
  pi.ingredient_name
HAVING SUM(pi.ingredient_quantity) <> 0
views.description: For each distinct ingredient, sum the ingredient_quantity across all delivered pizza ingredient instances, and include the ingredient name. Exclude ingredients whose summed total equals zero in the final filtering step (filter can be applied here or at final combine).

views.name: orders_cohort
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  r.order_id AS order_id,
  'completed' AS order_status,
  r.pickup_time AS order_date
FROM pizza_clean_runner_orders r
WHERE r.cancellation IS NULL OR TRIM(r.cancellation) = ''

semantic_filters.order_status: exclude canceled orders; only completed orders retained

views.description: Select the cohort of orders that are completed (i.e., exclude canceled orders). Keep order-level identifiers and status needed to join to order items.

views.name: pizza_items_cohort
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  pcco.order_id AS order_id,
  pcco.order_id || '-' || pcco.pizza_id AS order_item_id,
  pn.pizza_name AS pizza_type,
  1 AS quantity,
  NULL AS item_unit_price
FROM pizza_clean_customer_orders pcco
JOIN pizza_names pn ON pcco.pizza_id = pn.pizza_id
WHERE pn.pizza_name IN ('Meatlovers', 'Vegetarian')
views.description: Select order line items that represent pizzas of interest (Meat Lovers or Vegetarian). Keep item-level identifiers, the order_id they belong to, the pizza type/name, quantity, and any item-level price or unit indicator if present.

views.name: extra_toppings_per_item
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  order_id AS order_item_id,
  SUM(extras_count) AS extra_topping_count
FROM pizza_get_extras
GROUP BY order_id
views.description: For each pizza item (order_item_id), count the number of extra toppings associated with that item. Only include toppings that are extra add-ons linked to pizza items.

views.name: pizza_revenue_items
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  c.order_id,
  c.order_id || '-' || ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY c.order_id ORDER BY c.order_id) AS order_item_id,
  pn.pizza_name AS pizza_type,
  COALESCE(1, 1) * 1 AS quantity, /* placeholder; quantity per item assumed 1 from clean orders grain */
  CASE
    WHEN pn.pizza_name = 'Meatlovers' THEN 12
    WHEN pn.pizza_name = 'Vegetarian' THEN 10
    ELSE NULL
  END AS unit_price_assigned,
  COALESCE(et.extra_topping_count, 0) AS extra_topping_count,
  (CASE
     WHEN pn.pizza_name = 'Meatlovers' THEN 12
     WHEN pn.pizza_name = 'Vegetarian' THEN 10
     ELSE 0
   END + COALESCE(et.extra_topping_count, 0) * 1) * COALESCE(1, 1) AS item_total_revenue
FROM pizza_clean_customer_orders c
JOIN pizza_names pn ON pn.pizza_id = c.pizza_id
LEFT JOIN extra_toppings_per_item et ON et.order_item_id = c.order_id
WHERE pn.pizza_name IN ('Meatlovers', 'Vegetarian')
views.description: Join the completed orders to the pizza items and their extra-topping counts; filter to only the Meat Lovers and Vegetarian pizzas, and compute per-item-level revenue components using canonical unit prices (Meat Lovers = 12, Vegetarian = 10) plus $1 per extra topping, multiplied by the item quantity. Produce one row per order_item to be summed later.

views.name: word_rows
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  words AS word,
  length(words) AS length
FROM word_list
views.description: Select the set of words to consider from the source dictionary/repository, keeping each word as a distinct row along with its full original case-sensitive text and length.

views.name: filtered_words
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  words AS word,
  length(words) AS length
FROM
  word_list
WHERE
  (length(words) = 4 OR length(words) = 5)
  AND substr(words, 1, 1) = 'r'
views.description: Filter words to only those whose length is 4 or 5 and whose first character is the lowercase letter 'r'.

views.name: word_signature
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  wl.words AS word,
  LENGTH(wl.words) AS length,
  (
    SELECT GROUP_CONCAT(ch, '')
    FROM (
      SELECT substr(wl.words, pos, 1) AS ch
      FROM (
        SELECT 1 AS pos UNION ALL SELECT 2 UNION ALL SELECT 3 UNION ALL SELECT 4 UNION ALL SELECT 5
        UNION ALL SELECT 6 UNION ALL SELECT 7 UNION ALL SELECT 8 UNION ALL SELECT 9 UNION ALL SELECT 10
        UNION ALL SELECT 11 UNION ALL SELECT 12 UNION ALL SELECT 13 UNION ALL SELECT 14 UNION ALL SELECT 15
        UNION ALL SELECT 16 UNION ALL SELECT 17 UNION ALL SELECT 18 UNION ALL SELECT 19 UNION ALL SELECT 20
        UNION ALL SELECT 21 UNION ALL SELECT 22 UNION ALL SELECT 23 UNION ALL SELECT 24 UNION ALL SELECT 25
        UNION ALL SELECT 26 UNION ALL SELECT 27 UNION ALL SELECT 28 UNION ALL SELECT 29 UNION ALL SELECT 30
        UNION ALL SELECT 31 UNION ALL SELECT 32 UNION ALL SELECT 33 UNION ALL SELECT 34 UNION ALL SELECT 35
        UNION ALL SELECT 36 UNION ALL SELECT 37 UNION ALL SELECT 38 UNION ALL SELECT 39 UNION ALL SELECT 40
      ) positions
      WHERE pos <= LENGTH(wl.words)
      ORDER BY ch
    )
  ) AS signature
FROM word_list wl
views.description: For each word produce a canonical anagram signature: a case-sensitive ordering of its characters (e.g., sort characters) to identify anagram groups without changing original case.

views.name: anagram_counts
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  w.words AS word,
  LENGTH(w.words) AS length,
  (
    SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT w2.words)
    FROM word_list w2
    WHERE LENGTH(w2.words) = LENGTH(w.words)
      AND (
        SELECT GROUP_CONCAT(ch, '')
        FROM (
          SELECT SUBSTR(w2.words, idx, 1) AS ch
          FROM (
            SELECT 1 AS idx UNION ALL SELECT 2 UNION ALL SELECT 3 UNION ALL SELECT 4 UNION ALL SELECT 5
            UNION ALL SELECT 6 UNION ALL SELECT 7 UNION ALL SELECT 8 UNION ALL SELECT 9 UNION ALL SELECT 10
            UNION ALL SELECT 11 UNION ALL SELECT 12 UNION ALL SELECT 13 UNION ALL SELECT 14 UNION ALL SELECT 15
            UNION ALL SELECT 16 UNION ALL SELECT 17 UNION ALL SELECT 18 UNION ALL SELECT 19 UNION ALL SELECT 20
            UNION ALL SELECT 21 UNION ALL SELECT 22 UNION ALL SELECT 23 UNION ALL SELECT 24 UNION ALL SELECT 25
            UNION ALL SELECT 26 UNION ALL SELECT 27 UNION ALL SELECT 28 UNION ALL SELECT 29 UNION ALL SELECT 30
            UNION ALL SELECT 31 UNION ALL SELECT 32 UNION ALL SELECT 33 UNION ALL SELECT 34 UNION ALL SELECT 35
            UNION ALL SELECT 36 UNION ALL SELECT 37 UNION ALL SELECT 38 UNION ALL SELECT 39 UNION ALL SELECT 40
          ) AS idxs
          WHERE idx <= LENGTH(w2.words)
          ORDER BY ch
        )
      ) =
      (
        SELECT GROUP_CONCAT(ch, '')
        FROM (
          SELECT SUBSTR(w.words, idx, 1) AS ch
          FROM (
            SELECT 1 AS idx UNION ALL SELECT 2 UNION ALL SELECT 3 UNION ALL SELECT 4 UNION ALL SELECT 5
            UNION ALL SELECT 6 UNION ALL SELECT 7 UNION ALL SELECT 8 UNION ALL SELECT 9 UNION ALL SELECT 10
            UNION ALL SELECT 11 UNION ALL SELECT 12 UNION ALL SELECT 13 UNION ALL SELECT 14 UNION ALL SELECT 15
            UNION ALL SELECT 16 UNION ALL SELECT 17 UNION ALL SELECT 18 UNION ALL SELECT 19 UNION ALL SELECT 20
            UNION ALL SELECT 21 UNION ALL SELECT 22 UNION ALL SELECT 23 UNION ALL SELECT 24 UNION ALL SELECT 25
            UNION ALL SELECT 26 UNION ALL SELECT 27 UNION ALL SELECT 28 UNION ALL SELECT 29 UNION ALL SELECT 30
            UNION ALL SELECT 31 UNION ALL SELECT 32 UNION ALL SELECT 33 UNION ALL SELECT 34 UNION ALL SELECT 35
            UNION ALL SELECT 36 UNION ALL SELECT 37 UNION ALL SELECT 38 UNION ALL SELECT 39 UNION ALL SELECT 40
          ) AS idxs
          WHERE idx <= LENGTH(w.words)
          ORDER BY ch
        )
      )
      AND w2.words <> w.words
  ) AS anagram_count
FROM word_list w
views.description: Group words by signature and length, and for each word compute the count of other distinct words (same length and exact case-sensitive characters arrangement when permuted) that share the signature (exclude the word itself).
